Face Recognition: are these two photographs the same person?¶

The question: the legacy notebook was a Google Colab script. It mounted a Google Drive, installed the face_recognition library, turned a folder of "known" photographs into face encodings, compared each "unknown" photograph with them and printed which known people matched. It showed matches, but never counted how often it is right. How accurate is modern face verification on a standard benchmark? How much does a deep network add over classic descriptors? Where should the "same or different" threshold sit? What makes the rare mistakes happen? And how fragile is the system when the photograph is blurred, noisy, small or dark? We use Labeled Faces in the Wild (LFW) and its standard protocol: 6,000 pairs of photographs, half of the same person and half of different people, in 10 folds.

How this notebook works. Each section starts with a plain-English explanation, then the code, then a "how to read this" note.

  1. The analogy
  2. Setup
  3. Audit: the pairs
  4. Hypotheses and why we chose each test
  5. Finding, aligning and describing a face
  6. H1: does a deep network beat classic descriptors?
  7. H2: where should the threshold sit?
  8. H3: what makes the mistakes happen?
  9. H4: how fragile is it?
  10. H5: the worst mistakes
  11. Takeaways
  12. Limitations

Run it: uv run jupyter lab CV/face-recognition/face_recognition.ipynb, or Run All in any Jupyter. LFW (about 180 MB) and two small models (about 40 MB) download themselves on the first run. It takes about 35 minutes on a CPU (most of it is re-describing the photographs under eight different degradations).

1. 💡 The simple analogy¶

Imagine a border guard comparing a passport photograph with the person in front of him.

  • A naive guard compares the two pictures dot by dot, like laying one transparency on the other. A slightly different angle or a smile spoils it.
  • A trained guard has learnt a short "description" of a face (the shape of the eyes, the distance between them, the jaw) that stays the same when the lighting, the angle and the expression change. He decides "same person" if the two descriptions are close enough.
  • The threshold is how close is "close enough". Too strict and he turns away honest travellers; too lenient and he lets a look-alike through.
  • Bad conditions (a blurry photograph, a noisy camera, a face that is tiny in the frame) make the descriptions drift apart, and an honest traveller looks like a stranger.

2. Setup¶

What: imports and named constants. Why: one place for numbers like the seed, the number of folds (10) and the recommended threshold of the face model (a cosine similarity of 0.363) keeps the notebook reproducible and avoids "magic numbers".

DETECT_SCORE = 0.5

@contextlib.contextmanager
def silence_native_logs():
    """Hides messages that compiled libraries write straight to the terminal (file descriptor 2)."""
    sys.stderr.flush()
    saved, devnull = os.dup(2), os.open(os.devnull, os.O_WRONLY)
    os.dup2(devnull, 2)
    try:
        yield
    finally:
        os.dup2(saved, 2)
        os.close(devnull)
        os.close(saved)


def fmt_p(p: float) -> str:
    """Formats a p-value, showing values below floating-point precision honestly.

    Args:
        p: The p-value.

    Returns:
        A short string such as ``3.2e-08`` or ``< 1e-300``.
    """
    return "< 1e-300" if float(p) < 1e-300 else f"{float(p):.1e}"

3. Audit: the pairs¶

What: Labeled Faces in the Wild: 13,233 photographs of 5,749 famous people, taken from news photographs, with the standard pairs file for the verification test: 10 folds, each with 300 same-person and 300 different-person pairs. We read the pairs, count the distinct photographs and people, and check that the folds are separate people. Why: verification is about deciding for a pair, and the protocol keeps the people of one fold away from the others so that a model cannot memorise them.

Problems in the legacy notebook this replaces: it ran only on Google Colab (it mounted a Google Drive); it resized with the width and height swapped, which squashes every face; it took face_encodings(img)[0] without checking that a face was found, so a photograph with no detected face crashes it; and it had no ground truth, so it never measured how often a match was right.

In [2]:
for name, url in URLS.items():
    target = DATA_DIR / name
    if not target.exists():
        request = urllib.request.Request(url, headers={"User-Agent": "Mozilla/5.0"})
        with urllib.request.urlopen(request, timeout=300) as response:
            target.write_bytes(response.read())
if not (DATA_DIR / "lfw").exists():
    with tarfile.open(DATA_DIR / "lfw.tgz") as tf:
        tf.extractall(DATA_DIR, filter="data")


def read_pairs(path: Path) -> pd.DataFrame:
    """Reads the standard LFW pairs file (10 folds; same-person pairs first, then different).

    Args:
        path: ``pairs.txt``.

    Returns:
        One row per pair: ``fold``, ``same`` (1 or 0) and the two image paths.
    """
    lines = path.read_text().splitlines()
    n_folds, per_kind = (int(v) for v in lines[0].split())
    rows, cursor = [], 1
    for fold in range(n_folds):
        for _ in range(per_kind):  # same person
            name, a, b = lines[cursor].split()
            rows.append(
                (fold, 1, f"{name}/{name}_{int(a):04d}.jpg", f"{name}/{name}_{int(b):04d}.jpg")
            )
            cursor += 1
        for _ in range(per_kind):  # different people
            n1, a, n2, b = lines[cursor].split()
            rows.append((fold, 0, f"{n1}/{n1}_{int(a):04d}.jpg", f"{n2}/{n2}_{int(b):04d}.jpg"))
            cursor += 1
    return pd.DataFrame(rows, columns=["fold", "same", "a", "b"])


pairs = read_pairs(DATA_DIR / "pairs.txt")
unique = sorted(set(pairs["a"]) | set(pairs["b"]))
people = sorted({p.split("/")[0] for p in unique})
people_a = pairs["a"].str.split("/").str[0]
people_b = pairs["b"].str.split("/").str[0]
overlap = [
    len(
        (set(people_a[pairs["fold"] == f]) | set(people_b[pairs["fold"] == f]))
        & (set(people_a[pairs["fold"] != f]) | set(people_b[pairs["fold"] != f]))
    )
    for f in range(N_FOLDS)
]
print(
    f"{len(pairs):,} pairs in {N_FOLDS} folds ({int(pairs['same'].sum()):,} same person, "
    f"{int((1 - pairs['same']).sum()):,} different people)"
)
print(f"{len(unique):,} distinct photographs of {len(people):,} people")
print(
    f"Images are {cv2.imread(str(DATA_DIR / 'lfw' / unique[0])).shape[1]} x "
    f"{cv2.imread(str(DATA_DIR / 'lfw' / unique[0])).shape[0]} pixels, faces roughly centred"
)
print(
    f"People who appear in a fold and also in another fold: {min(overlap)} to {max(overlap)} "
    "per fold"
)

6,000 pairs in 10 folds (3,000 same person, 3,000 different people)
7,701 distinct photographs of 4,281 people
Images are 250 x 250 pixels, faces roughly centred
People who appear in a fold and also in another fold: 0 to 0 per fold

How to read this:

  • 6,000 pairs in 10 folds (3,000 same person, 3,000 different people) from 7,701 distinct photographs of 4,281 people. Every photograph is a 250 x 250 pixel colour image with the face roughly in the middle.
  • The folds are made of separate people: no person appears in two folds, so the threshold chosen on nine folds is judged on people it has never seen.
  • A model that guessed would score 50%.

4. Hypotheses and why we chose each test¶

# Question H₀ (nothing interesting) Hₐ Test
H1 Does a deep face network beat classic descriptors (local binary patterns, raw pixels)? Same verification accuracy The network is better 10-fold accuracy (the standard protocol); paired Wilcoxon test across folds; AUC, equal error rate and true accept rate at a fixed false accept rate
H2 Does a threshold chosen on the data beat the model's recommended fixed one, and how stable is it? Same accuracy Differs Paired Wilcoxon across folds; spread of the chosen thresholds
H3 Are the mistakes related to the quality of the photographs (face size, blur, detector confidence)? No relation Wrong pairs have weaker faces Mann-Whitney U and Cliff's δ
H4 Is the system robust to blur, noise, darkness, small faces and compression? Same accuracy as on clean photographs Lower Exact McNemar test on the same 6,000 pairs

Why these tests? The standard LFW protocol picks the threshold on nine folds and tests on the tenth, so each fold gives one honest accuracy; the paired Wilcoxon test compares two methods fold by fold (with 10 folds the smallest possible p-value is 0.002). A degraded and a clean run score the same pairs, so the exact McNemar test, which looks only at the pairs where the two runs disagree, is the right test.

5. Finding, aligning and describing a face¶

What: three steps for each photograph.

  1. Find the face: OpenCV's YuNet detector. If it finds several, we take the face closest to the middle of the photograph (LFW is centred on its subject); if it finds none we use a box in the middle with typical landmark positions, so every pair can be scored.
  2. Align and crop: rotate and scale the face so the eyes, nose and mouth are in fixed places, in a 112 x 112 crop.
  3. Describe it, three ways, from the same crop: SFace (a small deep network from OpenCV that turns the face into 128 numbers), LBP histograms (a classic descriptor: counts of local brightness patterns on a 7 x 7 grid) and raw pixels (the grey values, shrunk to 56 x 56). A pair's similarity is the cosine of its two descriptions: near 1 means very alike.

The two classic baselines are deliberately simple and untuned; they show what "no deep learning" gets you, not the best a classic method can do.

In [3]:
with silence_native_logs():
    detector = cv2.FaceDetectorYN.create(
        str(DATA_DIR / "face_detection_yunet_2023mar.onnx"),
        "",
        (250, 250),
        score_threshold=DETECT_SCORE,
    )
    recognizer = cv2.FaceRecognizerSF.create(
        str(DATA_DIR / "face_recognition_sface_2021dec.onnx"), ""
    )


def describe(image: np.ndarray) -> dict:
    """Finds the most central face in an image and describes it three ways.

    Args:
        image: BGR image.

    Returns:
        A dict with the SFace embedding (``deep``, 128 numbers, unit length), two classic
        descriptors from the aligned face (``pixels`` and ``lbp``), the detector score, the face
        size in pixels, a blur measure and whether a face was really found. If YuNet finds no
        face, the middle of the image is used as the face (so every pair can be scored).
    """
    height, width = image.shape[:2]
    detector.setInputSize((width, height))
    _, faces = detector.detect(image)
    found = faces is not None and len(faces) > 0
    if found:
        centre = np.array([width / 2, height / 2])
        face = min(faces, key=lambda f: np.linalg.norm(f[:2] + f[2:4] / 2 - centre))
    else:  # fall back to a box in the middle of the image with typical landmarks
        w = h = min(width, height) * 0.45
        x, y = (width - w) / 2, (height - h) / 2
        face = np.array(
            [
                x,
                y,
                w,
                h,
                x + 0.3 * w,
                y + 0.38 * h,
                x + 0.7 * w,
                y + 0.38 * h,
                x + 0.5 * w,
                y + 0.6 * h,
                x + 0.33 * w,
                y + 0.8 * h,
                x + 0.67 * w,
                y + 0.8 * h,
                0.0,
            ],
            np.float32,
        )
    aligned = recognizer.alignCrop(image, face)
    deep = recognizer.feature(aligned).ravel()
    gray = cv2.cvtColor(aligned, cv2.COLOR_BGR2GRAY)
    pixels = cv2.resize(gray, (56, 56)).astype(np.float32).ravel()
    pixels = (pixels - pixels.mean()) / (np.linalg.norm(pixels - pixels.mean()) + 1e-9)
    codes = local_binary_pattern(gray, 8, 1, "uniform")
    cells = [
        np.bincount(codes[r : r + 16, c : c + 16].astype(int).ravel(), minlength=10)
        for r in range(0, FACE_SIZE, 16)
        for c in range(0, FACE_SIZE, 16)
    ]
    lbp = np.concatenate(cells).astype(np.float32)
    lbp = np.sqrt(lbp / lbp.sum())  # a square root makes histogram distances behave
    return {
        "deep": deep / np.linalg.norm(deep),
        "pixels": pixels,
        "lbp": lbp / np.linalg.norm(lbp),
        "score": float(face[14]),
        "size": float(face[2]),
        "found": found,
        "blur": float(cv2.Laplacian(gray, cv2.CV_64F).var()),
    }


def describe_all(degrade=None) -> dict[str, dict]:
    """Describes every photograph in the pairs, optionally after degrading it.

    Args:
        degrade: A function from BGR image to BGR image, or None for the clean photographs.

    Returns:
        The description of each photograph, by path.
    """
    out = {}
    for path in unique:
        image = cv2.imread(str(DATA_DIR / "lfw" / path))
        out[path] = describe(degrade(image) if degrade else image)
    return out


with silence_native_logs():
    clean = describe_all()
found_share = np.mean([d["found"] for d in clean.values()])
print(f"Described {len(clean):,} photographs; YuNet found a face in {found_share:.2%} of them")
print(
    "Face width in pixels: median {:.0f}, 5th percentile {:.0f}".format(
        np.median([d["size"] for d in clean.values()]),
        np.percentile([d["size"] for d in clean.values()], 5),
    )
)

Described 7,701 photographs; YuNet found a face in 100.00% of them
Face width in pixels: median 93, 5th percentile 82

How to read this:

  • Every photograph has a face: YuNet found a face in 100.00% of the 7,701 photographs, so no fallback was needed.
  • The faces are small, but sharp enough: the median face is 93 pixels wide (5th percentile 82 pixels).

6. H1: does a deep network beat classic descriptors?¶

What: for each method, the standard 10-fold test: for each fold, pick the accuracy-maximising threshold on the other nine folds and score the held-out fold. We also compute the AUC, the equal error rate (where false accepts equal false rejects) and the true accept rate at a false accept rate of 1% and 0.1%, and test SFace against each baseline across folds. Why: the deep network is the one we would use, and we should see what it buys.

In [4]:
def similarity(descriptions: dict[str, dict], method: str) -> np.ndarray:
    """Similarity of each pair (higher means more likely the same person).

    Args:
        descriptions: Photograph descriptions from ``describe_all``.
        method: ``deep`` (cosine of SFace embeddings), ``pixels`` (cosine of normalised grey
            pixels) or ``lbp`` (cosine of square-rooted local-binary-pattern histograms).

    Returns:
        One score per pair.
    """
    a = np.stack([descriptions[p][method] for p in pairs["a"]])
    b = np.stack([descriptions[p][method] for p in pairs["b"]])
    return (a * b).sum(1)


def best_threshold(scores: np.ndarray, same: np.ndarray) -> float:
    """The threshold that gives the highest accuracy on the given pairs."""
    order = np.argsort(scores)
    s, y = scores[order], same[order]
    # predicting 'same' above position i: correct = different pairs below + same pairs above
    below_diff = np.cumsum(1 - y)
    above_same = y.sum() - np.cumsum(y)
    accuracy = (below_diff + above_same) / len(y)
    k = int(np.argmax(accuracy))
    return float(s[k] if k == len(s) - 1 else (s[k] + s[k + 1]) / 2)


def ten_fold(scores: np.ndarray) -> pd.DataFrame:
    """The LFW protocol: for each fold, pick the threshold on the other nine, test on this one."""
    same = pairs["same"].to_numpy()
    rows = []
    for fold in range(N_FOLDS):
        test = (pairs["fold"] == fold).to_numpy()
        t = best_threshold(scores[~test], same[~test])
        pred = (scores[test] > t).astype(int)
        rows.append({"fold": fold, "threshold": t, "accuracy": float((pred == same[test]).mean())})
    return pd.DataFrame(rows)


METHODS = {
    "deep": "SFace embedding (deep network)",
    "lbp": "LBP histograms (classic)",
    "pixels": "Raw pixels (naive)",
}
same = pairs["same"].to_numpy()
clean_scores = {m: similarity(clean, m) for m in METHODS}
folds = {m: ten_fold(s) for m, s in clean_scores.items()}
rows = []
for m, label in METHODS.items():
    acc = folds[m]["accuracy"]
    fpr, tpr, _ = roc_curve(same, clean_scores[m])
    eer_index = np.argmin(np.abs(fpr - (1 - tpr)))
    rows.append(
        {
            "method": label,
            "accuracy": acc.mean(),
            "SE": acc.std(ddof=1) / np.sqrt(N_FOLDS),
            "AUC": roc_auc_score(same, clean_scores[m]),
            "EER": fpr[eer_index],
            "TAR at FAR 1%": float(np.interp(0.01, fpr, tpr)),
            "TAR at FAR 0.1%": float(np.interp(0.001, fpr, tpr)),
        }
    )
board = pd.DataFrame(rows).set_index("method")
print(board.round(4).to_string())
base_acc = folds["deep"]["accuracy"].to_numpy()
for m in ("lbp", "pixels"):
    other = folds[m]["accuracy"].to_numpy()
    wil = stats.wilcoxon(base_acc, other)
    print(
        f"SFace minus {METHODS[m]}: {np.mean(base_acc - other):+.3f} accuracy; better in "
        f"{int((base_acc > other).sum())} of {N_FOLDS} folds; paired Wilcoxon p = "
        f"{fmt_p(wil.pvalue)}"
    )

                                accuracy      SE     AUC     EER  TAR at FAR 1%  TAR at FAR 0.1%
method                                                                                          
SFace embedding (deep network)    0.9935  0.0012  0.9988  0.0087         0.9927           0.9880
LBP histograms (classic)          0.5737  0.0059  0.6071  0.4257         0.0670           0.0167
Raw pixels (naive)                0.6192  0.0074  0.6673  0.3757         0.0767           0.0150
SFace minus LBP histograms (classic): +0.420 accuracy; better in 10 of 10 folds; paired Wilcoxon p = 2.0e-03

for (m, label), color in zip(METHODS.items(), [TEAL, ORANGE, GREY], strict=True):
    fpr, tpr, _ = roc_curve(same, clean_scores[m])
    ax.plot(
        fpr * 100,
        tpr * 100,
        color=color,
        lw=2.5,
        label=f"{label} (AUC {roc_auc_score(same, clean_scores[m]):.3f})",
    )
ax.plot([0, 100], [0, 100], color=GREY, ls="--", lw=1)
ax.set_xlabel("False accept rate: different people accepted as the same (%)")
ax.set_ylabel("True accept rate: same person recognised (%)")
ax.set_title(
    "A trained face network beats classic descriptors by a wide margin",
    loc="left",
    fontweight="bold",
    fontsize=11,
)
ax.legend(loc="lower right", fontsize=9)
fig.tight_layout()
fig.savefig(OUT_DIR / "01_roc.png", dpi=150)

How to read this:

Method Accuracy AUC Equal error rate Accepts at 1% false accepts
SFace embedding 99.35% (SE 0.12) 0.9988 0.9% 99.3%
Raw pixels 61.92% (SE 0.74) 0.667 37.6% 7.7%
LBP histograms 57.37% (SE 0.59) 0.607 42.6% 6.7%
  • The deep network is dramatically better: 99.35% of pairs right against 57% and 62% for the classic descriptors (which are not far above the 50% of a coin). It is better in all 10 folds (+42.0 and +37.4 points; paired Wilcoxon p = 0.002, the smallest value 10 folds can give). We reject H₀.
  • At a strict false accept rate it still works: at 0.1% false accepts (3 of 3,000 different-person pairs) SFace accepts 98.8% of the same-person pairs; the baselines accept 1.5% to 1.7%.
  • The two baselines use the aligned crop but fail on the changes of pose, expression and lighting of news photographs; that is why a learned description is needed.

7. H2: where should the threshold sit?¶

What: the face model comes with a recommended cosine threshold of 0.363. We compare it with the threshold the 10-fold protocol picks on the data (nine folds, judged on the tenth), look at how stable the chosen threshold is across folds, and at the two score distributions: the similarity of the 3,000 same-person pairs and the 3,000 different-person pairs. At each threshold we count false accepts (different people called the same) and false rejects (the same person called different). Why: the threshold decides which mistake you make; a legacy script usually hides it in a default.

In [6]:
deep = clean_scores["deep"]
tuned = folds["deep"]
fixed_acc = np.array(
    [
        (
            (deep[(pairs["fold"] == f).to_numpy()] > SFACE_THRESHOLD).astype(int)
            == same[(pairs["fold"] == f).to_numpy()]
        ).mean()
        for f in range(N_FOLDS)
    ]
)
print(
    f"Fixed recommended threshold {SFACE_THRESHOLD}: accuracy {fixed_acc.mean():.4f} "
    f"(SE {fixed_acc.std(ddof=1) / np.sqrt(N_FOLDS):.4f})"
)
print(
    f"Threshold chosen on the other nine folds: accuracy {tuned['accuracy'].mean():.4f}; "
    f"the thresholds are {tuned['threshold'].min():.3f} to {tuned['threshold'].max():.3f} "
    f"(mean {tuned['threshold'].mean():.3f}, SD {tuned['threshold'].std(ddof=1):.3f})"
)
wil = stats.wilcoxon(tuned["accuracy"], fixed_acc)
print(
    f"Tuned minus fixed: {np.mean(tuned['accuracy'] - fixed_acc):+.4f}; "
    f"paired Wilcoxon p = {fmt_p(wil.pvalue)}"
)
same_scores, diff_scores = deep[same == 1], deep[same == 0]
print(
    f"Similarity of same-person pairs: median {np.median(same_scores):.3f} "
    f"(5th-95th percentile {np.percentile(same_scores, 5):.3f} to "
    f"{np.percentile(same_scores, 95):.3f}); different people: median "
    f"{np.median(diff_scores):.3f} ({np.percentile(diff_scores, 5):.3f} to "
    f"{np.percentile(diff_scores, 95):.3f})"
)
for name, t in [("recommended", SFACE_THRESHOLD), ("tuned (mean)", tuned["threshold"].mean())]:
    far = float((diff_scores > t).mean())
    frr = float((same_scores <= t).mean())
    print(
        f"At the {name} threshold {t:.3f}: false accepts {far:.2%} of different-person pairs, "
        f"false rejects {frr:.2%} of same-person pairs"
    )
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(9, 4.8))
bins = np.linspace(-0.2, 1.0, 61)
ax.hist(
    diff_scores,
    bins=bins,
    color=ORANGE,
    alpha=0.65,
    density=True,
    label="different people (3,000 pairs)",
)
ax.hist(
    same_scores, bins=bins, color=TEAL, alpha=0.65, density=True, label="same person (3,000 pairs)"
)
ax.axvline(SFACE_THRESHOLD, color=NAVY, ls="--", lw=1.5, label=f"threshold {SFACE_THRESHOLD}")
ax.set_xlabel("Cosine similarity of the two face embeddings")
ax.set_ylabel("Share of pairs")
ax.set_title(
    "The two kinds of pair are separated, but they overlap in the middle",
    loc="left",
    fontweight="bold",
    fontsize=11,
)
ax.legend()
fig.tight_layout()

Similarity of same-person pairs: median 0.665 (5th-95th percentile 0.455 to 0.821); different people: median 0.081 (-0.061 to 0.228)
At the recommended threshold 0.363: false accepts 0.07% of different-person pairs, false rejects 1.53% of same-person pairs
At the tuned (mean) threshold 0.313: false accepts 0.33% of different-person pairs, false rejects 0.90% of same-person pairs

How to read this:

  • The two kinds of pair are far apart: same-person pairs have a median similarity of 0.665 (5th to 95th percentile 0.455 to 0.821); different-person pairs 0.081 (-0.061 to 0.228). The distributions overlap only a little, around 0.3.
  • The recommended threshold works well: accuracy 99.20% (SE 0.17) at 0.363, against 99.35% for the threshold chosen on the data: a gain of +0.15 points that is not significant (paired Wilcoxon p = 0.062). We do not reject H₀.
  • The chosen thresholds are stable: 0.308 to 0.332 across the ten folds (mean 0.313, SD 0.010), a little below the recommended value. A lower threshold trades the two mistakes: at 0.363, 0.07% of different-person pairs are accepted and 1.53% of same-person pairs rejected; at 0.313, 0.33% and 0.90%.
  • The lesson: the model's default is a sound choice; the question to ask is which mistake is worse for the application (a border gate and a photo album would pick different thresholds).

8. H3: what makes the mistakes happen?¶

What: using the out-of-fold decisions (each pair is judged with a threshold chosen on the other nine folds), we compare the wrong pairs with the right pairs on three quality measures of the worse of the two photographs: the face's width in pixels, the detector's confidence and the blur (the variance of the Laplacian: low means blurry). We use Mann-Whitney tests with Cliff's δ and look at accuracy by blur quarter. Why: knowing what goes wrong tells you what to fix: the camera, the lighting or the model.

In [7]:
pair_info = pd.DataFrame(
    {
        "same": same,
        "min_size": [
            min(clean[a]["size"], clean[b]["size"])
            for a, b in zip(pairs["a"], pairs["b"], strict=True)
        ],
        "min_blur": [
            min(clean[a]["blur"], clean[b]["blur"])
            for a, b in zip(pairs["a"], pairs["b"], strict=True)
        ],
        "min_score": [
            min(clean[a]["score"], clean[b]["score"])
            for a, b in zip(pairs["a"], pairs["b"], strict=True)
        ],
        "fold": pairs["fold"],
        "similarity": deep,
    }
)
oof_pred = np.zeros(len(pairs), int)
for f in range(N_FOLDS):
    test = (pairs["fold"] == f).to_numpy()
    oof_pred[test] = (deep[test] > tuned.loc[f, "threshold"]).astype(int)
pair_info["correct"] = oof_pred == same
print(
    f"Out-of-fold accuracy over all 6,000 pairs: {pair_info['correct'].mean():.4f} "
    f"({int((~pair_info['correct']).sum())} pairs wrong: "
    f"{int(((oof_pred == 0) & (same == 1)).sum())} same-person pairs rejected, "
    f"{int(((oof_pred == 1) & (same == 0)).sum())} different-person pairs accepted)"
)
for column, label in [
    ("min_size", "smaller face width (pixels)"),
    ("min_score", "weaker detection score"),
    ("min_blur", "blurrier face (Laplacian variance)"),
]:
    ok, bad = (
        pair_info.loc[pair_info["correct"], column],
        pair_info.loc[~pair_info["correct"], column],
    )
    mw = stats.mannwhitneyu(bad, ok)
    delta = 2 * mw.statistic / (len(ok) * len(bad)) - 1
    print(
        f"  {label}: wrong pairs median {bad.median():.2f} vs right pairs {ok.median():.2f}; "
        f"Mann-Whitney p = {fmt_p(mw.pvalue)}, Cliff's delta = {delta:+.2f}"
    )
pair_info["blur band"] = pd.qcut(
    pair_info["min_blur"], 4, labels=["blurriest", "blurry", "sharp", "sharpest"]
)
print(
    "Accuracy by blur quarter (blurriest to sharpest): "
    + ", ".join(f"{v:.3f}" for v in pair_info.groupby("blur band", observed=True)["correct"].mean())
)

Out-of-fold accuracy over all 6,000 pairs: 0.9935 (39 pairs wrong: 29 same-person pairs rejected, 10 different-person pairs accepted)
  smaller face width (pixels): wrong pairs median 88.58 vs right pairs 89.78; Mann-Whitney p = 2.5e-01, Cliff's delta = -0.11
  weaker detection score: wrong pairs median 0.92 vs right pairs 0.92; Mann-Whitney p = 1.0e-03, Cliff's delta = -0.30
  blurrier face (Laplacian variance): wrong pairs median 119.87 vs right pairs 128.67; Mann-Whitney p = 6.0e-01, Cliff's delta = -0.05
Accuracy by blur quarter (blurriest to sharpest): 0.993, 0.991, 0.995, 0.995

How to read this:

  • Only 39 of 6,000 pairs are wrong (99.35% correct): 29 same-person pairs rejected and 10 different-person pairs accepted.
  • The quality measures barely separate them: the smaller face width is 88.6 pixels in wrong pairs against 89.8 in right ones (p = 0.25, δ = -0.11); the blur measure 119.9 against 128.7 (p = 0.60, δ = -0.05). Accuracy by blur quarter, from the blurriest to the sharpest, is 99.3%, 99.1%, 99.5%, 99.5%: no clear trend.
  • The detector's confidence differs a little: the wrong pairs have a slightly weaker detection score (medians equal to two decimals, 0.92; p = 0.001, δ = -0.30, a small to moderate effect), as expected if odd poses and expressions are harder to find and to match.
  • We cannot reject H₀ for size and blur, and only weakly for detector confidence: on these news photographs, which are all sharp enough and of similar size, the rare errors are not about the photograph quality. Section 10 shows what they are about. With only 39 errors, the test has little power.

9. H4: how fragile is it?¶

What: we damage both photographs of every pair in eight ways and score the same 6,000 pairs again, with the thresholds fixed from the clean photographs: Gaussian blur (σ = 2 and 4 pixels), the whole photograph shrunk to a half and a quarter (a person further away; the face drops from 93 to about 46 and 23 pixels), a dark photograph (40% brightness), sensor noise (σ = 25) and heavy JPEG compression (quality 10). For each, the accuracy, the AUC and the two mistake rates, and an exact McNemar test against the clean run. Why: a benchmark of clean news photographs is the easiest case; real cameras are not.

In [8]:
def blur(sigma: float):
    """A degradation: Gaussian blur."""
    return lambda im: cv2.GaussianBlur(im, (0, 0), sigma)


def shrink(factor: float):
    """A degradation: the whole photograph is shrunk (the face is further from the camera)."""
    return lambda im: cv2.resize(im, None, fx=factor, fy=factor, interpolation=cv2.INTER_AREA)


def darken(gain: float):
    """A degradation: a darker photograph."""
    return lambda im: np.clip(im.astype(np.float32) * gain, 0, 255).astype(np.uint8)


def noisy(sigma: float):
    """A degradation: Gaussian sensor noise."""
    noise_rng = np.random.default_rng(SEED)
    return lambda im: np.clip(im + noise_rng.normal(0, sigma, im.shape), 0, 255).astype(np.uint8)


def jpeg(quality: int):
    """A degradation: heavy JPEG compression."""
    return lambda im: cv2.imdecode(
        cv2.imencode(".jpg", im, [cv2.IMWRITE_JPEG_QUALITY, quality])[1], cv2.IMREAD_COLOR
    )


CONDITIONS = {
    "clean": None,
    "blur 2": blur(2),
    "blur 4": blur(4),
    "half size": shrink(0.5),
    "quarter size": shrink(0.25),
    "dark (40%)": darken(0.4),
    "noise 25": noisy(25),
    "JPEG quality 10": jpeg(10),
}
rows, correct_by = [], {}
for name, fn in CONDITIONS.items():
    with silence_native_logs():
        d = clean if fn is None else describe_all(fn)
    s = similarity(d, "deep")
    pred = np.zeros(len(pairs), int)
    for f in range(N_FOLDS):
        test = (pairs["fold"] == f).to_numpy()
        pred[test] = (s[test] > tuned.loc[f, "threshold"]).astype(int)
    correct_by[name] = pred == same
    found = np.mean([x["found"] for x in d.values()])
    rows.append(
        {
            "condition": name,
            "face found": found,
            "accuracy": correct_by[name].mean(),
            "AUC": roc_auc_score(same, s),
            "different accepted": float(((pred == 1) & (same == 0)).sum() / (same == 0).sum()),
            "same rejected": float(((pred == 0) & (same == 1)).sum() / (same == 1).sum()),
        }
    )
robust = pd.DataFrame(rows).set_index("condition")
print(robust.round(3).to_string())
for name in list(CONDITIONS)[1:]:
    a, b = correct_by["clean"], correct_by[name]
    mc = mcnemar(
        [[int((a & b).sum()), int((a & ~b).sum())], [int((~a & b).sum()), int((~a & ~b).sum())]],
        exact=True,
    )
    print(
        f"{name}: clean right and degraded wrong on {int((a & ~b).sum())} pairs, the reverse on "
        f"{int((~a & b).sum())}; exact McNemar p = {fmt_p(mc.pvalue)}"
    )

How to read this:

Condition Accuracy Different people accepted Same person rejected
Clean 99.4% 0.3% 1.0%
Darkness (40%) 99.2% 0.4% 1.2%
Half size (face about 46 px) 99.3% 0.8% 0.7%
Blur, σ = 2 98.6% 0.8% 2.0%
JPEG quality 10 97.4% 0.5% 4.7%
Quarter size (face about 23 px) 96.8% 0.8% 5.7%
Blur, σ = 4 92.4% 1.4% 13.8%
Sensor noise, σ = 25 91.6% 1.1% 15.8%
  • Darkness and half size do no harm: 99.2% and 99.3% (McNemar p = 0.23 and 0.52: no significant change).
  • Strong blur and noise hurt a lot: accuracy falls to 92.4% (σ = 4 blur) and 91.6% (noise), and almost all of the new errors are same-person pairs rejected (13.8% and 15.8% of them). The honest traveller looks like a stranger. Against the clean run the system loses 427 and 479 pairs and gains 9 and 13 (p below 1e-100). In the noisy photographs the detector also misses 1.2% of the faces.
  • Shrinking to a quarter size (a face about 23 pixels wide) costs 2.6 points (165 pairs lost, 11 gained; p = 2e-36). Heavy compression costs 2.0 points (p = 2e-25).
  • We reject H₀ for blur, noise, quarter size and compression; not for darkness and half size. The system fails quietly: the false accept rate grows only a little (0.3% to 1.4%) while the false reject rate grows 15 times: with a fixed threshold, bad images are turned away, not mistaken for others.
  • A caveat for the legacy script: it shrank every frame by a factor of 4 before detection. Our quarter-size test is a similar shrink.

10. H5: the worst mistakes¶

What: the photographs of the two highest-scoring false accepts (different people the system called the same) and the two lowest-scoring false rejects (the same person called different), with the similarity score. Why: "wrong" is not a single thing, and the examples say what a better system would have to learn.

Ten highest-scoring false accepts: Lennox Lewis / Monte Kiffin; Janela Jara / Pa Kou Hang; Alan Dreher / Francisco Santos; Andrew Sabey / Greg Rusedski; Rolf Eckrodt / Teresa Heinz Kerry; Eric Lloyd / Jessica Alba; Bob Hayes / Zhu Rongji; Colleen OClair / Tom Hanusik; Mike Martz / William Burns; Alisha Richman / Miguel Rosseto

How to read this:

  • The two worst false accepts are not obvious look-alikes: the two pairs of strangers score only 0.41 (Lennox Lewis and Monte Kiffin) and 0.37 (Janela Jara and Pa Kou Hang), barely above the 0.363 threshold. The second pair shows two faces with strained, unusual expressions: the model reads the expression as much as the person.
  • The two worst false rejects probably are not mistakes of the model: the "same person" pairs of Cristina Fernandez and Jim OBrien score 0.05 and the photographs look like two different people each (two women of different looks; a white-haired man with an open mouth and a bald man). LFW is known to contain a few identity-label errors, where two people share a name; these are probably two of them.
  • So the 29 false rejects are a mixture of real failures (pose, expression, age) and noisy labels; we did not check all of them by hand. This is a reminder that 99.35% is measured against labels that are themselves imperfect.
  • No mistake is a photograph-quality problem in the sense of H3: all of the photographs are sharp and of normal size; a better threshold cannot fix them.

11. 🎯 Takeaways¶

  1. Modern face verification is very accurate on clean photographs: 99.35% of 6,000 LFW pairs (SE 0.12%) with the standard protocol, AUC 0.9988, and a 98.8% accept rate at 0.1% false accepts.
  2. A deep network is essential: classic descriptors (LBP histograms, raw pixels) reach only 57% to 62%, barely above chance, and lose in all 10 folds.
  3. The recommended threshold is already a good one: 99.20% against 99.35% for one chosen on the data (p = 0.062); the chosen thresholds sit between 0.31 and 0.33.
  4. Rare mistakes are not about photograph quality: 39 wrong pairs; size and blur do not separate them from the right pairs.
  5. But degraded images fail quietly: blur (σ = 4) and noise drop accuracy to 92% and 91.6%, with 14% to 16% of same-person pairs rejected and almost no extra false accepts; a quarter-size face loses 2.6 points; darkness and half size cost nothing.
  6. Measure under your own conditions: a recogniser tuned on clean news photographs is a different system on a noisy webcam.

12. ⚠️ Limitations¶

  • LFW is an easy benchmark: celebrities photographed by news agencies, mostly frontal, well lit and sharp. Accuracy at 99.4% does not carry over to surveillance cameras or large databases (the attendance project shows what a bigger roster does).
  • Only 6,000 pairs and 39 mistakes, so subgroup tests (H3) have little power, and the p-values for 10 folds have a floor of 0.002.
  • The baselines are simple and untuned, so the +42 points is a comparison with weak descriptors, not with the best classic methods.
  • No demographic analysis: LFW has no age, gender or skin-tone labels and is known to be unbalanced (mostly adult men, mostly lighter skin); error rates can differ across groups and were not measured here.
  • The degradations are synthetic, applied to the photographs after the fact, and the threshold was not re-tuned for them.
  • One detector and one recogniser (YuNet and SFace); other models, such as larger ones, behave differently.
  • The pair protocol is verification (same or different), not identification among many people, and not open-set recognition.
  • Face recognition raises privacy and consent issues that no benchmark measures; do not use it on people who have not agreed.
